Notebooklm صار اقوى 🔥



 صار يتحول من “أداة تلخص ملفاتك” إلى “وكيل بحث” يشتغل داخل ملفاتك.



يعني قبل كان NotebookLM غالبًا: يرفع له PDF / مقالات / ملاحظات → تسأله → يجاوبك من المصادر.



الآن الترقية تقول إنه صار أقوى في:



1. Agentic chat

يعني المحادثة مو بس سؤال وجواب. يقدر يشتغل بخطوات: يبحث داخل مستنداتك، يربط المعلومات، يطلع نتيجة منظمة، ويكمل المهمة كأنه مساعد بحث.



2. Advanced reasoning

صار أفضل في المسائل المعقدة: مقارنة، تحليل، تلخيص عميق، استخراج أفكار، بناء حجج، وربط مصادر كثيرة.



3. New output formats

Audio Overview، Mind Map، Flashcards، Infographics، Tables.

 وبعض التغطيات ذكرت أن التحديثات الجديدة توسع المخرجات إلى ملفات مثل PDF وExcel وPowerPoint وCSV ورسومات/صور. 



4. Searching your docs

: “Searching your docs...”

يعني مو بس يقرأ الملف الحالي، بل يبحث داخل مصادر النوتبوك كلها ويجمع لك الجواب منها.



الخلاصة القوية:



NotebookLM صار أقرب إلى Research Agent مبني على مستنداتك.

مو مجرد summarizer.



لو عندك كتب، عقود، تقارير، ملفات مشروع، محاضرات، أو ملاحظات — تقدر تخليه يبني لك: دراسة، ملخص تنفيذي، جدول مقارنة، mind map، flashcards، عرض تقديمي، أو تحليل من مصادر محددة.

📢 Shared Task on Arabic Sentence Segmentation @ the 4th Arabic NLP Conference (araseg.aramlab.ai/) 📢



The shared task focuses on segmenting Arabic documents into coherent sentences. Given an Arabic document as input, participating systems must identify sentence boundaries throughout the text. The task is formulated as a binary token classification problem, where models predict whether a sentence boundary follows each token.

There’s a ton of interest in custom model tuning as agents reach production and scale up. Here is how we made Databricks Knowledge Assistant 3x faster using our new Instructed Retriever model trained end-to-end to do parallel test-time compute. It’s rolling out to customers now!


Databricks AI Research (@DbrxMosaicAI)



Most agentic search systems get better by thinking longer: more tool calls, more reason-act loops, each step waiting on the last. Quality goes up, but so does latency.



Instructed-Retriever-1 takes a different route. Instead of scaling test-time compute sequentially, it scales it in parallel. One retrieval-specialized model fans the work out: it generates multiple query and filter formulations to widen recall, then reranks the merged evidence with a multi-pivot reranker to sharpen precision. Both stages run at once, so searching more broadly no longer means searching more slowly.



The result inside Knowledge Assistant: search time drops more than 3x and answer time 2x, with time to first token around two seconds, and no drop in quality (it matches Claude Sonnet 4.5 retrieval quality on KARLBench). For the people using it, that means far less waiting between question and answer, the freedom to ask more follow-ups, and more of the knowledge base actually surfaced. Rolling out to all customers now, with no reconfiguration.

Here are 5 distance metrics in vector search.



But how do you choose the right one?

• L1 (Manhattan): sum of absolute differences, exact kNN only with no HNSW support

• L2 (Euclidean): straight-line distance, the safe default for most models

• Cosine similarity: angle between vectors, magnitude ignored

• Dot product: same ranking as cosine on normalized vectors, less compute

• Max inner product: dot product without the normalization constraint



Most teams default to cosine and move on. That works until your model outputs non-normalized vectors, and suddenly dot product or max inner product is the better fit.

Jeff Bezos: “People who are right a lot change their mind a lot”



“Because of AI, new technologies, and all the dynamism in the world, so many things are changing — and they’re changing rapidly,” Jeff observes.



The best solution he’s found for dealing with this rapid change is “thinking long-term” because it forces you to ask yourself, “What are the points of stability?” and “What is not going to change?”



He continues:



“One of the things that changes very slowly is customer needs. So you can build a strategy around customer needs. That will have durability.”



When building Amazon, for example, Jeff built the company around the customer needs of fast delivery, low prices, and vast selection.



“The technologies will change. Your competitive set will change. Everything will change, except those customer needs,” Jeff argues.



And it’s this idea that is behind Jeff’s core idea of “Be stubborn on the vision, and flexible on the details.”



He explains:



“You have to be [flexible on the details] because the world is changing and so you change your mind. I’ve noticed that people who are right a lot change their mind a lot. People who are wrong a lot are very stubborn on the details.”

For coding harnesses, I use Codex as my main driver (via 2 x $200/month ChatGPT subscriptions) with Claude for a bunch of more specialized work (1 x $200/month).



My setup evolves constantly, so it feels like there’s never a good moment to stop and say, “This is the way to do it,” but I am trying to at least capture a snapshot for you.



Not just for coding.



For *everything*.



Almost anything I used to use Make or N8N for... or GPTs, prompts, all that stuff, it's now just *here* as skills and workflows and SOPs and Obsidian vaults (folders full of markdown text files) that connect to all of it.



Real soon I hope to publish what I’m calling my Personal OS.



I’m barely in the actual ChatGPT or Claude web chat anymore. I’m in this.



Personal OS will be a snapshot of what I use daily. I'm trying to get it to set itself up for you depending on your needs and what you have already. It'll come with the business-focused skills and things and I think the coding stuff will be an optional upgrade.



I’ve been working for weeks to turn this in this template that sets itself up, and a short 1-hour course about these agent harness things and how to use them to be a 10x or 100x of whatever you want to be.



People have been asking for it, so I’m delivering.



Here’s what my typical day looks like:



After getting the kiddos off to school and the dog walked, I’m running Codex and Claude apps across two monitors, along with some Obsidian vaults and a few web browsers.



I’ll be managing 3-5 workstreams at a time, with agents performing research, coding up new features, exploring ideas, managing my task list, checking my email, investigating bugs, building a little hobby app on the side… whatever I think they can do for me.



Maybe 30% of the messages I send invoke one or more skills. This is where prompt engineering has evolved to, although a skill is often much more than a prompt.



The two skills I use the most are called “Now what? Figure out a plan” and “Fresh eyes”. You can probably guess a little about what they do.



So anything I do often becomes a skill, and it’s something I work with the agent to improve over time. Any time I use the skill and I don’t like how it went, I might update it. 95% of the time I tell the AI to update its own skill based on what I want. A by-hand pass over a skill often reveals ways to improve it, in minor ways, but usually it’s not necessary unless it’s a core file like your root AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md files.



Not everything can be AI-driven, obviously, so I'm regularly stopping, reviewing, planning, figuring stuff out. That can be the hardest transition, like going 100 mph on the freeway and having to suddenly get out of the car and start walking every once and a while.



But it can be good to slow down and go outside sometimes, right?



SO.



Will I start creating content again regularly?



It’s hard to say definitively. I love building and I’m hoping to continue that. But I’ve discovered so much, it feels wasteful not to share. So I’m trying to get back into it.



This is a crazy moment in history.

​

What's possible today wasn't possible 6 months ago.

​

I’m doing everything I can to capture it. To play the role I want to play in it as best I can.



But boy-oh-boy, even with 3 mega subscriptions and 5 agents running all day, I never can seem to get all the work done. But that’s maybe because I’m aiming for 10-100x bigger goals than I ever have before.



Hope you’re well.

David has studied the minds of more generational company builders than anyone alive, from Jesus of Nazareth to Jensen Huang. 



I sat down with him to reverse engineer the psychological frameworks of history's greatest titans.



6 Lessons on the Unfiltered Reality of Iconic Founders.



1. Taste is real, and it starts with shutting up and actually listening.



2. On Negative Self-Talk: Many elite CEOs are fueled in their early days by a dark, chaotic mind and intense self-criticism. They categorically refuse to sleep on their wins, obsessing over everything that is currently broken. I was guilty of this at Hubspot. To survive a multi-decade career without self-destructing, that initial fuel source must eventually convert from negative anxiety into a love for the craft.



3. We need to stop trying to heavily manage or over-advise elite entrepreneurial talent. The greatest founders are irrepressible forces of nature who will relentlessly hunt down the specific knowledge and frameworks they need to win. They are not passively discovered by the market or by venture capitalists; VCs can't help them out of a bad year. They violently force the world to recognize their existence.



4.  Small egos don't build big companies. Elite founders are driven by control, not money. Money is just a side effect.



5.  Co-Founder Dynamics: Despite the modern dogma that you need a balanced co-founding team to succeed, historical precedent shows that a singular driving force almost always takes over. From Henry Ford operating as an autocrat to Steve Jobs refounding Apple alone, the equal partnership rarely stands the ultimate test of time. Even brilliant minds like Charlie Munger recognized they had to deliberately subjugate their own massive egos to support a singular talent like @WarrenBuffett .



6.  Focus is the whole game: "Mute the world and build your own" as he says.  True focus is your willingness to say no to incredibly good ideas because they distract from the truly great ones.
